April 29, 2026

The Honorable Debbie-Anne A. Reese
Secretary
Federal Energy Regulatory Commission
888 First Street NE
Washington, DC 20426

       RE:     Southwest Power Pool, Inc., Docket No. ER26-1323-____
               Submission of Response to Request for Additional Information

Dear Secretary Reese:

        Pursuant to the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s (“Commission” or
“FERC”) letter issued on March 30, 2026,1 in this proceeding, Southwest Power Pool, Inc.
(“SPP”) submits additional information2 concerning the filing it submitted on February 10,
2026,3 in Docket No. ER26-1323. SPP respectfully requests that the Commission issue an
order in this proceeding as early as practicable to enable SPP to prepare to receive requests
for Conditional High Impact Large Load Service (“CHILLS”).

I.     BACKGROUND

        On February 10, 2026, SPP submitted revisions to its Open Access Transmission
Tariff4 to add the proposed CHILLS that will allow High Impact Large Loads (“HILL”) to
be served with non-firm conditional transmission service.



1
       Sw. Power Pool, Inc., Deficiency Letter, Docket No. ER26-1323-000 (March 30,
       2026) (“Deficiency Letter”).
2
       SPP is attaching one, unmodified tariff record to this filing as required by the
       Commission. Electronic Tariff Filings, 130 FERC ¶ 61,047, at PP 3-8 (2010)
       (stating an amendment filing must include at least one tariff record even though a
       tariff revision might not otherwise be required).
3
       Submission of Tariff Revisions to Add Conditional High Impact Large Load
       Service of Southwest Power Pool, Inc., Docket No. ER26-1323-000 (Feb. 10, 2026)
       (“CHILLS Filing”).
4
       Southwest Power Pool, Inc., Open Access Transmission Tariff, Sixth Revised
       Volume No. 1 (“Tariff”). References in this answer to “Tariff” refer to the version
       of SPP’s Tariff currently in effect. “Proposed Tariff” refers to a version reflecting
       revisions proposes in this proceeding. All capitalized terms not otherwise defined
       in this answer shall have the definitions assigned by the Tariff.
 The Honorable Debbie-Anne A. Reese
April 29, 2026
Page 2

       Several parties filed motions to intervene.5

       Advanced Energy United,6 ITC Great Plains, LLC,7 the Solar Energy Industries
Association,8 and the Southwest Power Pool Transmission Owner Group9 filed comments
in support of the CHILLS Filing.

        The Southwest Power Pool Market Monitoring Unit (“MMU”) filed comments
stating it takes no position regarding the necessity of SPP’s proposal, but the Commission
should approve the proposal as a just and reasonable way to effectuate SPP’s goals.10

       Associated Electric Cooperative, Inc. (“AECI”) filed comments regarding the
impact of CHILLS on affected systems, coordination between SPP and affected system
operators, and the proposed Curtailment procedures.11




5
       Interventions were filed by: Advanced Energy United; Basin Electric Power
       Cooperative; Constellation Energy Generation, LLC; Electric Power Supply
       Association; Enchanted Rock, LLC; Geronimo Power, LLC; Kansas Electric
       Power Cooperative, Inc.; Louisiana Public Service Commission; Municipal Energy
       Agency of Nebraska; Omaha Public Power District; Public Citizen, Inc.; Solar
       Energy Industries Association; Southwest Power Pool Market Monitoring Unit;
       Southwest Power Pool Transmission Owner Group (comprised of American
       Electric Power Service Corporation; Evergy Kansas Central, Inc., Evergy Metro,
       Inc., and Evergy Missouri West, Inc.; Oklahoma Gas and Electric Company, and
       Xcel Energy Services Inc.); Sunflower Electric Power Corporation; Western Area
       Power Administration; Western Farmers Electric Cooperative.
6
       Comments of Advanced Energy United, Docket No. ER26-1323-000 (Mar. 3,
       2026).
7
       Motion to Intervene and Supporting Comments of ITC Great Plains, LLC, Docket
       No. ER26-1323-000 (Mar. 3, 2026).
8
       Comments of the Solar Energy Industries Association in Support, Docket No.
       ER26-1323-000 (Mar. 3, 2026).
9
       Comments of the Southwest Power Pool Transmission Owner Group, Docket No.
       ER26-1323-000 (Mar. 3, 2026).
10
       Comments of the Southwest Power Pool Market Monitoring Unit, Docket No.
       ER26-1323-000 (Mar. 3, 2026) (“MMU Comments”).
11
       Motion to Intervene and Comments of Associated Electric Cooperative, Inc.,
       Docket No. ER26-1323-000 (Mar. 3, 2026) (“AECI Comments”).
 The Honorable Debbie-Anne A. Reese
April 29, 2026
Page 3

       Enchanted Rock, LLC filed a limited protest regarding proposed language that is
applicable during Emergency Conditions and other specified circumstances.12

        On March 20, 2026, SPP submitted its answer in response to comments and limited
protest filed in this proceeding.13

       In the Deficiency Letter, the Commission directed SPP to provide additional
information necessary to process the filing. The Commission required responses be
submitted within thirty (30) days of the date of the Deficiency Letter.

        In Attachment 1 to this filing, SPP submits its responses to the specific questions
raised in the Deficiency Letter.

II.    CONCLUSION

       For all of the reasons discussed in the CHILLS Filing and this instant filing, the
Commission should accept the Proposed Tariff revisions as just and reasonable. SPP
requests that the Commission issue an order in this docket as early as practicable to enable
SPP to prepare to receive requests for CHILLS.

Attachment 1
SPP’s Response to Deficiency Letter




                 1
 Question 1:
      SPP proposes three avenues by which a transmission customer can obtain CHILLS:
      Attachments AQ, AX, and BC. Please explain when an eligible customer must submit
      a CHILLS application relative to when it must submit a request for a delivery point
      addition or modification to be studied under Attachments AQ, AX, or BC and whether
      additional Tariff revisions are needed to clarify this timeframe.

Response to 1:

      Under the current Tariff, an entity can submit a request for a delivery point addition or
      modification under Attachment AQ and Attachment AX, but at the same time must also
      submit its application for Network Integration Transmission Service (Part III, Section 29.2
      of the Tariff) or Firm Point-to-Point Transmission Service (Part II, Section 17.1 of the
      Tariff). This is the same for CHILLS. In the CHILLS process, a Transmission Customer
      can request to add or modify a delivery point pursuant to Attachments AQ, AX, and BC,
      but it must at the same time provide an application for the CHILLS pursuant to Part VII,
      Section 47.1 of the Proposed Tariff. Consistent with the current Tariff, there is no need for
      additional Tariff revisions to clarify this time frame. The CHILLS application and
      submission of a delivery point addition or modification are separate, independent steps in
      obtaining CHILLS and do not necessarily follow the same timeline. Although separate
      processes, both the application under Part VII and the request pursuant to Attachments AQ,
      AX, and BC are necessary to enable the establishment of a delivery point to be served by
      CHILLS.




                                               2
 Question 2:
       In proposed Part VII, section 47.1, SPP proposes that, after an eligible customer
       submits an application for CHILLS, SPP will acknowledge receipt of the application.
       The proposed Tariff language further provides that “[t]he acknowledgment must
       include a date by which a response, including a CHILLSA, will be sent to the Eligible
       Customer.”1 Additionally, proposed Part VII, section 47.2 (Time Requirements) of
       the Tariff provides that the evaluation of CHILLS requests will follow the timing
       requirements of Attachment P (Transmission Service Timing Requests). SPP’s
       proposed revisions to Attachment P provide that SPP will respond to the application
       “[a]t the Completion of Studies Outlined in Attachments AQ, AX, BA, and/or BC.”2
       Finally, proposed Part VII, section 44.3 (Service Agreements) of the Tariff states that
       SPP will provide a CHILLSA to an eligible customer when the customer first submits
       a completed CHILLS application. Please explain when SPP must tender a CHILLSA
       relative to when an eligible customer submits a valid CHILLS application and
       whether additional Tariff revisions are needed to clarify this timeframe.

Response to 2:

       There should be additional Tariff revisions to Part VII, Section 44.3 to ensure that it is clear
       when SPP must tender a Conditional High Impact Large Load Service Agreement
       (“CHILLSA”) to an Eligible Customer. To be consistent with other provisions of the
       Proposed Tariff, the first sentence in Part VII, Section 44.3 of the Proposed Tariff should
       be revised as follows: “The Transmission Provider will offer a standard form Conditional
       High Impact Large Load Service Agreement (CHILLSA), Addendum 2 to Attachment BA,
       to an Eligible Customer when it first submits a Completed Application for CHILLS
       pursuant to the Tariff at the completion of the studies outlined in Attachments AQ, AX,
       BA, and/or BC.” SPP agrees to submit on compliance revised Proposed Tariff records to
       reflect these changes, if so ordered by the Commission.




1
       Proposed Tariff, Part VII, § 47.1.
2
       Proposed Tariff, Att. P.

                                                  3
 Question 3:
       SPP proposes that Attachment BC apply “when it becomes necessary or desirable to
       establish a HILL delivery point or make changes in facilities at a HILL delivery point
       and the Network Customer or Transmission Customer does not have enough existing
       designated resources or planned designated resources to serve the increased load plus
       losses.”3 To be studied under the proposed Attachment BC, a transmission customer
       must have sufficient generation capacity to support the HILL that are not designated
       or planned designated resources.4

            a. In section 1.0 of Attachment BC, SPP proposes to require a network customer
               or transmission customer to submit a request for a HILL Delivery Point
               Limitations Assessment (HDPLA).5 In relevant part, SPP proposes:

                        The Network Customer or Transmission Customer will submit a
                        request for a HILL Delivery Point Limitations Assessment (“HDPLA”)
                        in writing to (a) the Transmission Provider and the Host Transmission
                        Owner as specified in Section 20 of the Network Operating Agreement
                        or (b) the Transmission Provider as specified in Section 8 of the Point-
                        To-Point Transmission Service Agreement, as applicable.6
                 Please explain whether a transmission customer requesting to establish or
                 modify a HILL delivery point must have an existing NOA or point-to-point
                 transmission service agreement and, if not, please explain how such a customer
                 would submit a HDPLA request under section 1.0 of Attachment BC.
Response to 3.a:

       Section 1.0 of Attachment BC was drafted using Section 1.0 of Attachment AQ as a guide.
       Pursuant to the current Tariff, only existing Transmission Customers or Network
       Customers are eligible to add or modify a delivery point pursuant to Attachment AQ, and
       therefore, the Transmission Customer or Network Customer has an existing SPP Network
       Operating Agreement7 or Form of Service Agreement for Firm Point-To-Point
       Transmission Service (“PTP Service Agreement”).8 Attachment BC as designed was not
       intended to be limited to existing Transmission Customers or Network Customers, so
       additional Tariff revisions are needed for Section 1.0 of Attachment BC to ensure that it is


3
       Proposed Tariff, Att. BC, § 1 (Requests for Establishment or Changes in High Impact Large Load (“HILL”)
       Local Delivery Facilities).
4
       Id.
5
       Id.
6
       Id.
7
       Tariff, Att. G.
8
       Tariff, Att. A.

                                                     4
        clear which customers are eligible to submit a HILL Delivery Point Limitations Assessment
       (“HDPLA”). To clarify eligibility under Attachment BC, the third sentence in Section 1.0
       of Attachment BC should be revised as follows: “The Network Customer or Transmission
       Customer will submit a request for a HILL Delivery Point Limitations Assessment
       (“HDPLA”) in writing to (a) the Transmission Provider and the Host Transmission Owner
       as specified in Section 20 of the Network Operating Agreement Network Integration
       Transmission Service or (b) the Transmission Provider as specified in Section 8 of the
       Point-To-Point Transmission Service Agreement, as applicable.” SPP agrees to submit on
       compliance revised Proposed Tariff records to reflect these changes, if so ordered by the
       Commission.

             b. In section 2.2 (Transmission System Study) of Attachment BC (High Impact
                Large Load Delivery Point Initial Assessment), SPP proposes that: “Upon
                receipt of the Request for a HDPLA, Transmission Provider will perform an
                assessment of the impact of the requested delivery point configuration change
                on the Transmission System . . . .”9 Later in section 2.2, SPP proposes that a
                HILL without designated resources or planned designated resources sufficient
                to cover the HILL will be subject to the HDPLA “described below.”10
                Proposed section 2.2 proceeds to describe the HDPLA as assessing the impacts
                to the transmission system “caused by requested HILL delivery point
                additions or modifications.”11 SPP further proposes that it will send a study
                report to the transmission customer and the host transmission owner. Please
                clarify whether the “assessment” described in section 2.2 of Attachment BC is
                the HDPLA. If not, please explain how that “assessment” and the HDPLA
                differ and explain whether SPP issues a separate study report for the HDPLA.

Response to 3.b:

       Yes, the “assessment” described in Section 2.2 of Attachment BC is the HDPLA.
             c. In section 2.2 of Attachment BC, SPP proposes:

                        The HDPLA study results do not establish a HILL delivery point for
                        load that cannot be served by currently planned generation and/or
                        Designated Resources until after the Transmission Customer or
                        Network Customer executes a Service Agreement pursuant to




9
       Proposed Tariff, Att. BC, § 2.2 (Transmission System Study).
10
       Id.
11
       Id.

                                                      5
                       Attachment AQ, Attachment AX, or Attachment BA of the Tariff, for
                      such load.12

              Please explain how and why a transmission customer proceeding through the
              Attachment BC study process would execute a service agreement under
              Attachment AQ or Attachment AX to establish a HILL delivery point for load
              that cannot be served by currently planned generation and/or designated
              resources. In your response, please explain why the CHILLSA, the service
              agreement pursuant to Attachment BA, would not be the appropriate service
              agreement to establish a HILL delivery point for such load.

Response to 3.c:

       A Transmission Customer taking transmission service at a HILL delivery point can serve
       that load either through firm service, CHILLS, or a combination of both. If the
       Transmission Customer is taking both firm service or CHILLS at the same delivery point,
       the firm load and CHILLS load must be separately metered. As the delivery point will be
       able to be served by a combination of firm or CHILLS service, an entity may be required
       to execute a service agreement under Attachment AQ, Attachment AX, and/or Attachment
       BA.

       The Attachment AQ study process allows a delivery point to be served firm transmission
       service, if that Transmission Customer has enough Designated Resources to serve the new
       load plus that Transmission Customer’s existing load. To effectuate the addition or
       modification of a delivery point studied under Attachment AQ, those delivery points are
       added to the Transmission Customer’s Network Integration Transmission Service
       Agreement or PTP Service Agreement. A Transmission Customer taking transmission
       service under Attachment AQ also has the ability to procure CHILLS for any portion of the
       transmission service granted that is affected by need to construct Network Upgrades. In
       that case, the entity would also execute a service agreement pursuant to Attachment BA.

       The Attachment AX study process allows a delivery point to be studied for firm
       transmission service if that Transmission Customer has planned resources to serve the new
       load. To effectuate this planned resource being studied to serve the new load, the
       Transmission Customer must execute a service agreement under Attachment AX.

       If a Transmission Customer does not have enough Designated Resources or any planned
       resources to serve a new load plus its existing load, the load can be studied initially pursuant
       to Attachment BC, if it meets all of the applicable requirements. If the Transmission


12
       Id.

                                                  6
 Customer is granted CHILLS service after all required studies, the customer must execute
a service agreement pursuant to proposed Attachment BA.

The following example outlines this possibility: A HILL delivery point is 300 MW. The
Transmission Customer has enough Designated Resources to support 100 MW of the HILL
delivery point. The Transmission Customer will execute a service agreement under
Attachment AQ for that 100 MW. The Transmission Customer also has a planned resource
that it desires to serve an additional 100 MW of the HILL delivery point. The Transmission
Customer will execute a service agreement under Attachment AX for that 100 MW. The
HILL delivery point could be further modified through Attachment BC to serve the
remaining 100 MW by CHILLS. In that situation, the Transmission Customer would
execute a CHILLSA pursuant to Attachment BA.




                                        7
 Question 4:
       The Commission’s pro forma Open Access Transmission Tariff includes provisions
       governing situations in which a transmission customer requests that a transmission
       service agreement be filed with the Commission unexecuted.13 Similarly, SPP’s
       existing Tariff provides such processes for its existing transmission services. 14 SPP
       states that it has substantially modeled CHILLS on existing transmission services
       because CHILLS shares similarities with such services.15 Please explain whether the
       proposed Tariff revisions allow eligible customers to request that the transmission
       provider file an unexecuted CHILLSA or unexecuted CHILLS Operating Agreement
       with the Commission and, if not, why the absence of such provisions is just and
       reasonable and not unduly discriminatory or preferential.16

Response to 4:

       The absence of such provisions are just and reasonable and not unduly discriminatory or
       preferential because CHILLS customers are not similarly situated to Transmission
       Customers taking firm service under the Commission’s pro forma Open Access
       Transmission Tariff. SPP designed the CHILLS as a special long-term, non-firm
       transmission service that includes specific terms and conditions that enable SPP to provide
       this type of transmission service in addition to more traditional transmission service. SPP
       is not proposing to allow either SPP or the Transmission Customer the ability to file a
       CHILLSA unexecuted with the Commission.

       At this time, SPP does not see a need to be able to force a Transmission Customer to take
       the non-firm transmission service through filing the CHILLSA unexecuted if the
       Transmission Customer does not agree to take the service subject to the specific terms and
       conditions outlined for CHILLS. The Transmission Customer should also not be able to
       force SPP to provide this non-firm transmission service through an unexecuted CHILLSA
       if the Transmission Customer does not agree to conform to the terms and conditions
       outlined in the CHILLSA.




13
       Pro Forma Open Access Transmission Tariff, §§ 15.3 (Initiating Service in the Absence of an Executed
       Service Agreement), 29.1 (Condition Precedent for Receiving Service).
14
       Tariff, Part II, § 15.3 (Initiating Service in the Absence of an Executed Service Agreement), Part III, § 29.1
       (Condition Precedent for Receiving Service).
15
       CHILLS Filing at 30.
16
       If SPP proposes to allow eligible customers to request that the transmission provider file an unexecuted
       CHILLSA or unexecuted CHILLS Operating Agreement with the Commission, we note that SPP’s existing
       definition for “Service Commencement Date” only applies to executed Service Agreements and unexecuted
       agreements under sections 15.3 and 29.1 of the Tariff. Tariff, Part I, § 1.

                                                        8
 Question 5:
       Please explain how and under what conditions SPP will shed or curtail CHILLS, given
       that SPP equates CHILLS’s priority to non-firm point-to-point transmission service.
       In your response, please explain whether transmission loading relief procedures
       pursuant to Attachment R in the Tariff will apply to CHILLS curtailments, similar to
       non-firm point-to-point transmission service. If so, please state the priority level that
       would be assigned to CHILLS. Please also explain whether SPP will curtail CHILLS
       for economic reasons, similar to non-firm point-to-point transmission service.

Response to 5:

       CHILLs agree to be curtailable under the conditions described in Attachment AE, Sections
       2.22.1(c)17 and (d)18 of the Proposed Tariff depending on the capacity supporting the
       CHILL. None of these conditions in which a CHILL must be curtailable include for an
       economic reason. Curtailment or interruption of Service under Part II, Section 14.7 of the
       Tariff only applies to Non-Firm Point-To-Point Transmission Service.

       SPP uses Transmission Loading Relief (“TLR”) procedures for transaction service
       associated with an e-Tag. In the event that CHILLS involved use of an e-Tag, then TLR
       procedures could be used in the decision to curtail service. For these purposes, CHILLS
       has a priority equal to Monthly Non-Firm Point-To-Point Service as described in Part VII,
       Section 44.2 of the Proposed Tariff (Priority 5). If there is no e-Tag associated with the
       CHILLS, the CHILLS impact is considered with other market flow for TLR processes.




17
       Attachment AE, Section 2.22.1(c) of the Proposed Tariff states: “the CHILL must agree to be curtailable in
       the event of (1) transmission limitations, (2) system CHILL Curtailments (3) under Emergency Conditions,
       or (4) a Local Reliability Issue.”

18
       Attachment AE Section 2.22.1(d) of the Proposed Tariff states: “the CHILL must agree to be curtailable (1)
       when the sum of the available capacity for the supporting Resources is less than the CHILL, (2) due to
       transmission limitations, (3) due to a Local Reliability Issue, (4) due to an unfavorable net impact to the
       transmission system during system CHILL Curtailments, or (5) due to Emergency Conditions.”


                                                       9
 Question 6:
       In sections 5.1.2 (Day-Ahead Market Execution), 5.2.2 (Day-Ahead Reliability Unit
       Commitment Execution), and 6.1.2 (Intra-Day Reliability Unit Commitment
       Execution) of Attachment AE, SPP proposes revisions to various provisions governing
       manual resource commitments to include reductions of CHILLS.19 SPP proposes that
       it will manually commit or reduce a CHILL or CHILLS.20 SPP’s existing Tariff
       language provides that manual commitments will be verified by the market monitor
       (i.e., SPP MMU) though the process described in section 6.1.2.1 (Determination of
       Non-Discriminatory Manual Resource Selection).21 Please explain whether CHILL
       and CHILLS reductions, as provided for in Attachment AE, will be monitored for
       non-discriminatory treatment by the SPP MMU. If not, please explain why not. If
       so, please explain how the Tariff provides for this.
Response to 6:

       CHILL and CHILLS reductions, as provided for in Attachment AE will be monitored by
       the SPP MMU under its authority described in Attachment AG, Section 4.2. SPP clarified
       the MMU’s authority to monitor CHILL and CHILLS reductions in Section 4.2 of
       Attachment AG22 instead of in Attachment AE at the request of the MMU. During the
       stakeholder process, the MMU submitted comments recommending this more general
       approach as manual resource commitments, which are verified by the MMU, will be
       evaluated differently than CHILL curtailments. They described their changes as:
                 [W]e have an initial recommendation on the revised RR’s redlines relating
                 to the MMU monitoring for discriminatory CHILL curtailments. In the
                 latest RR, SPP inserted new language regarding the MMU verifying that
                 CHILL curtailments are non-discriminatory into Attachment AE Section
                 6.1.2.1, which deals with discriminatory manual resource commitments. We
                 do not believe this is the appropriate section to insert language on CHILL
                 curtailments because it creates confusion with the current language
                 covering manual resource commitments, which are distinct from CHILL
                 curtailments and will be evaluated differently. We recommend the RTO
                 remove the redlines in Section 6.1.2.1 of Attachment AE and instead include




19
       Proposed Tariff, Att. AE, §§ 5.1.2 (Day-Ahead Market Execution), 5.2.2 (Day-Ahead Reliability Unit
       Commitment Execution), and 6.1.2 (Intra-Day Reliability Unit Commitment Execution).
20
       See, e.g., Proposed Tariff, Att. AE, §§ 5.2.2(4) (Day-Ahead Reliability Unit Commitment Execution), 6.1.2(4)
       (Intra-Day Reliability Unit Commitment Execution).
21
       Proposed Tariff, Att. AE, § 6.1.2(1) (Intra-Day Reliability Unit Commitment Execution).
22
       Proposed Tariff, Att. AG, § 4.2(s).

                                                       10
              load curtailments in Section 4.2 of Attachment AG, which provides a non-
             exhaustive list of the items the MMU will monitor.23


     Specifying the monitoring of CHILL Curtailments as being within the MMU’s authority
     will give it clear authority to investigate CHILL Curtailments and handle this information
     in accordance with its other powers and duties.




23
     Southwest Power Pool Market Monitoring Unit, RR720 Conditional High Impact Large Load Comment
     Form (Dec. 11, 2025) posted at: https://www.spp.org/spp-documents-filings/?id=21069 (contained in zip file
     “RR720 Conditional High Impact Large Load).



                                                    11
 Question 7:
       SPP proposes that the CHILLS commencement date can be extended for up to one
       year if requested by the transmission customer and no later than 60 days before the
       commencement of CHILLS, but that such an extension will require a non-refundable
       annual reservation fee.24 SPP further proposes that it will release a transmission
       customer’s CHILLS Reserved Capacity if another transmission customer submits a
       completed application during the extension period that can only be satisfied by
       releasing part or all of the original transmission customer’s CHILLS Reserved
       Capacity, unless the original transmission customer pays “the CHILLS transmission
       rate for its CHILLS Reserved Capacity.”25 Please explain whether the required
       payment (i.e., “the CHILLS transmission rate for its CHILLS Reserved Capacity”)
       for an original transmission customer to keep its CHILLS Reserved Capacity during
       an extension period, when such CHILLS Reserved Capacity is needed to satisfy the
       request of a subsequent CHILLS applicant, is the CHILLS transmission rate for the
       entire term of the transmission customer’s CHILLS, the extension period, or some
       other term.

Response to 7:

       The original Transmission Customer is agreeing to and reaffirming its commitment to pay
       the full service term starting on the new Service Commitment Date. This payment will
       occur at the CHILLS monthly transmission rate. This is consistent with Part II, Section
       17.7 of the Tariff (Extensions for Commencement of Service) and consistent with Section
       17.7 of the Commission’s pro forma Open Access Transmission Tariff. For the original
       Transmission Customer to keep its CHILLS Reserved Capacity in this scenario, it must:
       (1) pay one month of the CHILLS monthly transmission rate; and (2) pay for the CHILLS
       at the rates for the applicable Zone at that time when the service commences.




24
       Proposed Tariff, Part VII, § 47.6 (Extensions for Commencement of Service).
25
       Proposed Tariff, Part VII, § 47.6 (Extensions for Commencement of Service).

                                                     12
 Question 8:
       SPP proposes a new Schedule 15 to provide the rates for CHILLS. SPP states that it
       modeled the rates for CHILLS on the existing rates for non-firm point-to-point
       transmission service, due to various similarities in the nature of both services, and
       adopts Schedule 11 (Base Plan Zonal Charge) charges similar to both point-to-point
       transmission service and NITS.26 However, SPP’s proposed Schedule 15 does not
       include the subregional charge contained in Schedule 11 in the rates for CHILLS.
       Please explain why SPP does not propose to include the subregional charge contained
       in Schedule 11 in the rates charged for CHILLS under proposed Schedule 15.

Response to 8:

       During the development of the language included in Section 15, SPP’s filing proposing to
       include subregional charges was still pending at the Commission (See Docket No. ER26-
       407). SPP agrees that Schedule 15 should include the subregional charge contained in
       Schedule 11 in the rates for CHILLS. To ensure that Section 15 includes subregional
       charges, SPP proposes to amend Schedule 15, paragraph 6, of the Proposed Tariff as
       follows:

                 6.      Base Plan Zonal Charges, Subregional Charge, and Region-
                 wide Charges: The Transmission Customer and Network Customer must
                 pay the applicable Schedule 11 zonal rate (per kilowatt) based upon the
                 Zone where the load is located, the applicable Schedule 11 Subregional
                 Charge (per kilowatt) based upon the Subregion where the load is located,
                 and the applicable Schedule 11 region-wide rate for CHILLS. The rates will
                 be the applicable point-to-point hourly rates for the specific on-peak or off-
                 peak hour of CHILLS usage. The hourly charges will be calculated using
                 hourly kilowatts as stated in Section 1 of Schedule 15. The total Schedule
                 11 zonal charge in any month for usage up to the CHILLS Reserved
                 Capacity will not exceed the Schedule 11 point-to-point zonal monthly rate
                 times the amount in kilowatts of CHILLS Reserved Capacity in such month.
                 The total Schedule 11 region-wide charge in any month for usage up to the
                 CHILLS Reserved Capacity will not exceed the Schedule 11 point-to-point
                 region-wide rate times the amount of kilowatts of CHILLS Reserved
                 Capacity in such month.

       SPP agrees to submit on compliance revised Proposed Tariff records to reflect these
       changes, if so ordered by the Commission.


26
        See, e.g., CHILLS Filing at 29-30. See also Tariff, Schedule 8 (Non-Firm Point-to-Point Transmission
        Service); Tariff, Schedule 9 (Network Integration Transmission Service).

                                                   13
 Question 9:
       SPP further proposes that, in the event a CHILLS customer exceeds its CHILLS
       Reserved Capacity amount at any point of delivery, the CHILLS customer must pay
       (in addition to the charges for the CHILLS capacity used) a penalty charge equal to:
       100% of the non-firm point-to-point transmission service charges under Schedules 8
       (Non-Firm Point-To-Point Transmission Service) and Schedule 11 for the period when
       the additional service was used during the month for the amount in excess of such
       capacity reservation. SPP proposes to compensate transmission owners for the
       service by allocating penalty revenues to them, similar to its existing practices for
       distributing penalties collected for overuse of non-firm point-to-point transmission
       service.27 However, SPP’s proposed compensation to transmission owners for overuse
       of CHILLS does not include the subregional charge under Schedule 11. Specifically,
       this proposed compensation to transmission owners will consist of 100% of the: (1)
       CHILLS charge; (2) base plan zonal charge; and (3) region-wide charge for the period
       for which the transmission owners have provided service.28 Please explain why SPP
       does not propose to include the subregional charge contained in Schedule 11 in the
       proposed penalty charged to a CHILLS customer that exceeds its CHILLS Reserved
       Capacity.

Response to 9:
       During the development of the language included in Part VII, Section 44.4, SPP’s filing
       proposing to include subregional charges was still pending at the Commission (See Docket
       No. ER26-407). SPP agrees that Section 44.4 of the Proposed Tariff should include the
       subregional charge contained in Schedule 11. To ensure that Section 44.4 includes
       subregional charges, SPP proposes to amend Section 44.4 of the Proposed Tariff as follows:

                 The Transmission Provider will compensate the Transmission Owners for
                 100% of the (i) CHILLS charge, (ii) Subregional Charge, (ii) (iii) Base Plan
                 Zonal Charge, and (iii) (iv) Region-wide Charge for the period for which
                 they have provided service.

       SPP agrees to submit on compliance revised Proposed Tariff records to reflect these
       changes, if so ordered by the Commission.




27
       Tariff, Part II, § 14.5 (Classification of Non-Firm Point-To-Point Transmission Service).
28
       Proposed Tariff, Part VII, § 44.4 (Classification of Conditional High Impact Large Load Service).

                                                       14
 Question 10:
       SPP states that when network load and a CHILL are located at the same point of
       delivery with behind-the-meter generation, the network load must be adjusted for any
       excess hourly generation above the CHILLS Reserved Capacity.29 SPP states that it
       is necessary to adjust the network load by adding the amount of excess hourly
       generation to ensure all generation and load amounts are properly addressed through
       settlement and to prevent any netting of loads reported for NITS.30 The SPP MMU
       contends that SPP’s formula for determining network load when CHILLS load and
       behind-the-meter generation are at the same delivery point is incorrect, and suggests
       that excess generation should simply be the generation above the actual CHILLS
       load, rather than the CHILLS Reserved Capacity.31 In its answer, SPP reiterates its
       use of CHILLS Reserved Capacity, but states that the exact nature of the adjustment
       can vary with the metering configuration and that the exact formula need not be in
       the Tariff.


           a. Please explain why SPP proposes to calculate the excess hourly generation of
              behind-the-meter generation in this arrangement based on the CHILLS
              Reserved Capacity rather than the actual CHILLS load.

Response to 10.a:

       Upon further review of the Tariff language initially filed by SPP as well as the MMU’s
       comments, SPP now proposes to modify the requirement by removing the final sentence
       of Section 17.0 of the CHILLSA and amending the immediately preceding sentence of that
       section as follows, if so ordered by the Commission:

               For instances where both Network Load and CHILLS load are located at the same
               point of delivery with Behind-The-Meter Generation, as defined in Attachment AE
               of the Tariff, the Network Load must be adjusted for any excess hourly generation
               above the CHILLS Reserved Capacity to (1) add the hourly output of any Behind-
               The-Meter Generation that is located on the Network Load side of the Network
               Integration Transmission Service (“NITS”) meter and is not behind a CHILLS
               meter, and (2) subtract the positive (inflow, or CHILLS load) or negative (outflow)
               amount registered on any CHILLS meter located behind the NITS meter.


29
       SPP proposes to calculate the excess hourly generation as follows: excess hourly generation = min(CHILLS
       load or CHILLS Reserved Capacity) + hourly generation amount (from behind-the-meter generator) –
       CHILLS Reserved Capacity. Proposed Tariff, Att. BA, Add. 1 (Form of Service Agreement for Conditional
       High Impact Large Load Service), § 17.0 (CHILLS Load).
30
       CHILLS Filing at 26.
31
       SPP MMU Comments at 3-4.

                                                     15
        In cases where the generator is located on the Network Load side of the NITS meter and is
       not behind a CHILLS meter, the output of such generator cannot be used to meet the
       CHILLS curtailment requirement because the generator is serving Network Load.
       However, if the CHILLS customer’s supporting Behind-The-Meter Generation is not so
       located, the generator could be used by the customer to meet its CHILLS curtailment
       requirement.

       With the adjustment of language proposed above, SPP intends to address the gross-up of
       Network Load when it is being offset by Behind-The-Meter-Generation, which serves to
       clarify that a generator located as described above cannot be used to both serve Network
       Load and meet a CHILLS curtailment requirement. In such case, it is only serving Network
       Load. SPP agrees to submit on compliance revised Proposed Tariff records to reflect the
       above changes, if so ordered by the Commission.

           b. Please explain how the adjustments can vary with the metering configuration.
              In your response, please provide examples of the adjustment with at least two
              different metering configurations.

Response to 10.b:

       As stated in response to question 10.a, SPP is proposing to remove the description of the
       adjustment that was contained in its initial filed Tariff language. Rather than providing
       examples of that adjustment, SPP provides below five examples of different metering
       configurations and describes in each case how the metered quantities are to be applied.
       The application in each of these cases is consistent with existing Tariff requirements
       regarding the reporting of Network Load.

       While the existing Tariff language for Network Load and associated generation32 and the
       proposed language for CHILLS load and associated generation require separate metering,
       the specific configuration of such metering is not specified. Therefore, the treatment of the
       metered quantities will vary, depending on the metering configuration, in order to
       appropriately gross up generation located on the Network Load side of a Network
       Integration Transmission Service (“NITS”) meter and to allow a CHILLS supporting
       generator that is not so located to be used in meeting curtailment directives.




32
       See Tariff, Att. F, Attachment 1, Section 2.0 (Network Loads) (Attachment F contains the Network Integration
       Transmission Service Agreement).

                                                       16
 Because the generator is located behind the NITS meter, the generator is serving Network
Load and the amount of generation is added to the NITS meter reading to quantify the total
amount of Network Load during the hour. In this case, the 150 MW from the NITS meter
is added to the 80 MW of generation to result in a total of 230 MW of Network Load in the
hour. The CHILLS load served by the transmission system in the hour is 100 MW. The
total power flow through the delivery point is 250 MW (150 MW plus 100 MW). Because
the CHILLS load served by the transmission system does not exceed the CHILLS Reserved
Capacity of 120 MW, there is no unreserved use in the hour and the CHILLS customer will
be billed for the 120 MW of CHILLS Reserved Capacity if there is no Curtailment of the
CHILL.




                                       17
 Because no generator is located behind the NITS meter, the Network Load is the 230 MW
recorded on the NITS meter. The actual load behind the CHILLS meter in this hour is 100
MW, of which 80 MW is provided by the generator and 20 MW is provided by the
transmission system. The total power flow through the delivery point is 250 MW (230
MW plus 20 MW). There is no unreserved CHILLS use in the hour and the CHILLS
customer will be billed for the 120 MW of CHILLS Reserved Capacity if there is no
Curtailment of the CHILL.




                                      18
 Because no generator is located behind the NITS meter, the Network Load is the 230 MW
recorded on the NITS meter. If the generator in this configuration is designated as a
CHILLS supporting resource pursuant to Attachment BA, Section 4.1 of the Proposed
Tariff, the output of the generator can be used to meet a CHILLS curtailment and the net
of the CHILLS meter and generator meter is used to verify compliance with any
curtailment directive. The total power flow through the delivery point is 250 MW (230
MW plus 100 MW, less 80 MW). There is no unreserved CHILLS use in the hour and the
CHILLS customer will be billed for the 120 MW of CHILLS Reserved Capacity if there is
no Curtailment of the CHILL.




                                       19
 Because the generator is located behind the NITS meter, the generator is serving Network
Load and the amount of generation should be added to the NITS meter reading to quantify
the total amount of Network Load during the hour. Furthermore, the 100 MW recorded on
the CHILLS meter must be subtracted in determining the amount of Network Load.
Therefore, the Network Load is calculated as 250 MW on the NITS meter plus 80 MW on
the generator meter, less 100 MW on the CHILLs meter, to result in 230 MW of Network
Load. Because the NITS meter also serves as the delivery point meter, the total power flow
through the delivery point is 250 MW. The CHILLS load of 100 MW does not exceed the
CHILLS Reserved Capacity of 120 MW, so there is no unreserved use in the hour and the
CHILLS customer will be billed for the 120 MW of CHILLS Reserved Capacity if there is
no Curtailment of the CHILL.




                                       20
 Because the generator is located behind the CHILLS meter, the generator is directly serving
CHILLS load. In the situation depicted, however, the generator output of 110 MW exceeds
the load behind the CHILLS meter by 10 MW. Furthermore, the CHILLS meter is located
behind the NITS meter, which means that its recorded amount must be subtracted from the
NITS meter amount to calculate the Network Load. Subtracting the negative 10 MW (a
negative amount here signifying outflow back through the CHILLS meter to serve the
Network Load) from the 220 MW recorded on the NITS meter results in a Network Load
amount of 230 MW. The total power flow through the delivery point is 220 MW. The
CHILLS load does not exceed the CHILLS Reserved Capacity of 120 MW, so there is no
unreserved use in the hour and the CHILLS customer will be billed for the 120 MW of
CHILLS Reserved Capacity if there is no Curtailment of the CHILL.




                                        21
 Question 11:
       In section 17.0 of the CHILLSA, SPP proposes the following:
               The actual hourly CHILLS load and any firm load, by delivery point, internal
               generation site, and point where power may flow to or from the Transmission
               Customer or Network Customer, with separate readings for each direction of
               flow, must be provided.33

       Please explain whether this proposed language establishes a metering requirement for
       network load in order to provide the “firm load” amounts. If the proposed language
       does establish such a requirement, please explain why SPP proposes to establish such
       a requirement in a CHILLSA to which the network load is not a party.

Response to 11:

       No, the proposed language does not establish a new “metering requirement for network
       load in order to provide the ‘firm load’ amounts.” Section 2.0 of Attachment 1 of the pro
       forma Network Integration Transmission Service Agreement34 already requires that
       Network Load be separately metered. Therefore, the requirement for separate metering of
       CHILLS load proposed in Section 17.0 of the CHILLSA parallels the requirement included
       for network load, and this requirement ensures that CHILLS load will remain distinct from
       Network Load.




33
       Proposed Tariff, Att. BA, Add. 1 (Form of Service Agreement for Conditional High Impact Large Load
       Service) (0.0.0), § 17.0 (CHILLS Load).
34
       Tariff, Att. F, Attachment 1, Section 2.0 (Network Loads).

                                                  22
 Question 12:
       The SPP MMU also suggests that SPP should reassess allowing Load Responsible
       Entities (LRE) to use the same capacity to cover a CHILL that is used to meet their
       resource adequacy requirement.35 Please explain whether the same capacity used to
       cover a CHILL is allowed to be used in an LRE’s workbook to meet an LRE’s resource
       adequacy requirement. In your response, please also explain whether CHILLs are
       included in forecasts of Net Peak Demand used to determine an LRE’s resource
       adequacy requirement.

Response to 12:

       If a Transmission Customer is granted firm transmission service to a HILL delivery point
       under Attachment AQ but they are limited in the amount of firm transmission service that
       can serve at HILL delivery point because of needed Network Upgrades, the Transmission
       Customer’s load at the HILL delivery point may be eligible to be served by CHILLS for
       that portion of the HILL delivery point that cannot be served on a firm basis until the
       Network Upgrades are in service. During the Attachment AQ study process, the
       Transmission Customer must demonstrate that it has sufficient Designated Resources to
       serve all of its current firm load plus the addition of the HILL delivery point, including
       losses. Similar to all other firm load delivery points, the HILL delivery point will be
       supported by all of the Transmission Customer’s Designated Resources.

       As it relates to SPP’s resource adequacy process, the HILL delivery point that is being
       served by firm transmission service will be included in the forecasts of the Transmission
       Customer’s (i.e. LRE) Net Peak Demand. Any portion of the HILL delivery point that is
       served by CHILLS is served on a non-firm basis and would not be included in an LRE’s
       Net Peak Demand.




35
       SPP MMU Comments at 2-4.

                                              23
 Question 13:
       In SPP’s proposed Schedule 15, there are two sections with the same section
       numbering: “4. Discounts” and “4. Real Power Losses.”36 Please explain why SPP
       proposes to assign two different sections the same section number.

Response to 13:

       SPP inadvertently listed both the “Discounts” section and the “Real Power Losses” section
       as Section 4 of Schedule 15 of the Proposed Tariff. SPP proposes to adjust the section
       numbering in Schedule 15 so that it states “4. Discounts” and “5. Real Power Losses.”
       Additionally, SPP proposes to revise the other section numbers after the “Real Power
       Losses” section in Schedule 15 to account for this change. SPP agrees to submit on
       compliance revised Proposed Tariff records to reflect these changes, if so ordered by the
       Commission.




36
       Proposed Tariff, Schedule 15 (Conditional High Impact Large Load Service).

                                                    24
 Question 14:
       Proposed section 2.22.2 (Resources Supporting a HILL or CHILL) of Attachment AE
       states that it applies to “Resources Supporting a HILL or a CHILL.”37 In proposed
       section 2.22.2(3) of Attachment AE, SPP proposes “Behind-The-Meter Generation
       supporting a HILL and registered in the Integrated Marketplace . . . .” 38 Please
       explain whether proposed section 2.22.2(3) also applies to a CHILL. If not, please
       explain why such provision is not applicable to a CHILL.
Response to 14:

SPP’s proposed Tariff definition of a CHILL is “The portion of a High Impact Large Load that is
eligible to connect to the Transmission System and receive CHILLS as defined in Attachment BA
and Part VII of this Tariff.”39 By definition, a CHILL must consist of at least a portion of a HILL.
Attachment AE, Section 2.22.2(3) of the Proposed Tariff applies to the entire HILL, including any
portion that is a CHILL. Therefore, Behind-The-Meter Generation may support a HILL taking
CHILLS.

If the Commission orders on compliance, SPP proposes to clarify Section 2.22.2(3) of Attachment
AE to specify that it applies to CHILLS.




37
       Proposed Tariff, Att. AE, § 2.22.2 (Resources Supporting a HILL or CHILL).
38
       Proposed Tariff, Att. AE, § 2.22.2(3) (Resources Supporting a HILL or CHILL).
39
       Proposed Tariff, Part I, § 1 – C-Definitions.
